The shape of the corpus

Two AI-specific treaties, five trade agreements with AI provisions, a stack of declarations and resolutions, technical standards, and a negotiation on autonomous weapons. The binding layer is thin; the political layer is dense.

Key point. There is no single international AI regime. There are overlapping regimes, with different obligations, different members and different legal force.

Binding or not

Binding Non-binding

What “binding” means here

A treaty in force, a trade agreement in force, European Union law and two general framework treaties. It does not mean the obligation is detailed: CETS 225 and the WAICO Agreement are not in force, and the AfCFTA is not yet in force.

Declarations, UN resolutions, recommendations, codes of conduct and technical standards are non-binding. They are not irrelevant: they set direction, create expectations and prepare the ground for later rules.

02 · Three poles?

Three poles?

The three-pole image is a shorthand from policy analysis, not a finding of this corpus. It was a working hypothesis, and the legal record does not support reading it as three blocs. International law classifies the act and the party; it does not classify States into poles.

Washington

Market-led model · political coalition

Pax Silica Declaration

26 signatories · 25 States + EU

The 2025 US-led declaration on secure AI and technology supply chains. It is non-binding and creates no treaty obligation. The United States also convened the 2023 military declaration (58 endorsers) and signed CETS 225, Bletchley and Seoul, but did not endorse Paris.

Beijing

State-led model · constituent treaty

WAICO Establishment Agreement

38 reported founding members · not in force

The 2026 treaty establishing the World AI Cooperation Organization, headquartered in Shanghai. It is the second AI-specific treaty in the corpus and is limited to the civilian domain. China's 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative remains the policy line; China endorsed Bletchley and Paris but did not sign CETS 225 or the military declaration.

Brussels / Strasbourg

Rights-based model · treaty and regulation

Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225)

21 signatures · 2 ratifications

One of two AI-specific treaties, binding once in force. The EU has signed and ratified; not all EU member States are individual signatories. The EU AI Act is the separate supranational layer.

The frame, not a legal category

“Poles” and “blocs” are terms of political analysis. International law asks which act — treaty, political commitment, resolution, recommendation — and which party — State or international organisation. The literature does not converge on a fixed number:

  • Regime complexity. The AI governance landscape has no focal institution and low hierarchy: the United States, China and the EU pursue competing preferences through overlapping institutions, producing fragmentation rather than a tripolar legal order (Geith, Lundgren & Tallberg, Global Studies Quarterly, 2026).
  • Three models, not three alliances. Comparative policy analysis describes an American market-driven model, a Chinese state-driven model and a European rights-driven model, but treats them as ideal types, not legal blocs (Mokry, Global Policy, 2024; Bradford, Digital Empires, 2023).
  • The number depends on the axis. Policy analysis in 2026 describes two consolidating architectures (US-led Pax Silica, China-led WAICO) plus a UN track without capacity, and notes that many States join multiple frameworks (CSIS, 2026). On a forum axis, the triad is UN commons / US club / China–Global South diffusion (Tiberghien, East Asia Forum, 2026).

The number of poles therefore depends on the axis chosen: regulatory model, institutional vehicle or diplomatic coalition. The record below tests the metaphor against the legal acts.

Cross-cutting

Paris 2025: China and India endorsed; the United States and the United Kingdom did not

The Paris Statement is endorsed by 63 States, the European Union and the African Union Commission. It is the broadest instrument in the corpus. Its list cuts across the US–China axis: China and India are in, the United States and the United Kingdom are out. That is a political alignment, not a legal bloc.

63endorsing States

Who stands where

Paris, Bletchley, Seoul, the military declaration and Pax Silica record political endorsement; CETS 225 and the WAICO Agreement record treaty signature. CETS 225 also records ratification; China's approval of WAICO is noted but no deposit is counted. “Signed” means signature without ratification; “Signed + ratified” means both. Data as of 23 November 2026; the military declaration list is dated 27 November 2024; Pax Silica as of 23 October 2026. The MFA reports 38 WAICO founding members; 37 are individually identified.

The overlap is the point. The United States and the United Kingdom signed CETS 225 without ratifying it, but did not endorse Paris. China and India endorsed Paris and Bletchley, but did not sign CETS 225 or the military declaration. France and Germany endorsed Paris and the military declaration, but are not recorded as individual signatories of CETS 225. Kazakhstan endorsed Paris and signed both Pax Silica and the WAICO Agreement; Brazil and South Africa signed WAICO but not Pax Silica; India and Japan signed Pax Silica but not WAICO. China's NPC approved ratification of WAICO on 6 November 2026, but no deposit was verified, so the matrix records signature only. Political alignment does not map onto treaty participation.

Note on Paris: the Élysée page lists 65 endorsers; the 19 February 2025 PDF lists 64; a contemporaneous Canadian release listed 60, including South Africa, the United Arab Emirates and the Holy See. The matrix follows the current Élysée list, which does not include South Africa; the discrepancy is recorded in the Paris record.

What follows legally. There is no single legal order to join or leave. A State can endorse a political declaration, sign a treaty, ratify it or join a military declaration independently, and the same State can sit in different camps on different instruments: Kazakhstan endorsed Paris and signed both Pax Silica and the WAICO Agreement. The three-pole image describes regulatory competition; it does not describe legal blocs.

03 · Seven maps

Who signs what

Seven instruments, seven legal acts. The colour records the act, not the degree of alignment. Non-participation is shown in the same neutral colour for every State.

Boundaries: Natural Earth 1:110m Admin 0 Countries, public domain. The maps do not imply recognition of boundaries or sovereignty. Labels are orientation only. “Endorsed” is used for political declarations, which create no treaty signature or ratification.

Selection. The seven maps cover the instruments in the corpus with a published State-level list and a distinct legal act: five political instruments and two treaties. Not mapped: instruments without a published State-level list, or where the act is not a signature, or where a map would add no information — the OECD and UNESCO recommendations, the EU AI Act, strategies, codes and company commitments, the bilateral UK–US MOU and US–EU TTC commitment, the separate Pax Silica deliverables (the June 2026 AI Opportunity Statement and the November 2026 San Francisco Declaration), and the digital trade agreements, whose membership follows trade-partner logic rather than AI-governance alignment.

04 · How we got here

Timeline

The corpus runs from the general framework of 1966 to the instruments of 2026. The chart counts instruments adopted per year; the timeline selects the turning points.

Years present in the corpus; the scale is not continuous.

  1. 1966-12-16
    ICCPR

    The general framework for civil and political rights.

  2. 1969-05-22
    VCLT

    The rules on the law of treaties.

  3. 2019-05-22
    OECD AI Recommendation (OECD/LEGAL/0449)

    The first intergovernmental standard dedicated to AI.

  4. 2021-11-23
    UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation (2021)

    AI ethics adopted by 193 States.

  5. 2023-02-16
    U.S.-led Political Declaration on military AI

    US-led political declaration on military AI.

  6. 2023-10-18
    China's Global AI Governance Initiative

    The Chinese proposal: sovereignty, development and a central UN role.

  7. 2023-10-30
    G7 Hiroshima AI Process Code of Conduct

    Voluntary code for advanced AI developers.

  8. 2023-11-01
    Bletchley Declaration

    28 States and the EU on frontier-model risk.

  9. 2024-03-21
    UNGA resolution 78/265 on AI systems for sustainable development

    First UN resolution on AI adopted by consensus.

  10. 2024-04-01
    UK–US AI Safety MOU

    A bilateral AI-safety MOU between the UK and US institutes.

  11. 2024-04-05
    U.S.–EU TTC AI Safety Dialogue

    The US–EU TTC statement commits the European AI Office and the US AI Safety Institute to a technical Dialogue.

  12. 2024-09-05
    CoE Framework Convention on AI (CETS No. 225)

    The only AI-specific treaty; not yet in force.

  13. 2024-09-22
    Pact for the Future, including the Global Digital Compact (A/RES/79/1)

    Pact for the Future and Global Digital Compact.

  14. 2025-02-11
    Paris AI Action Summit Statement

    The Paris Statement: China and India endorsed; the United States and the UK did not.

  15. 2026-11-20
    CCW GGE on LAWS — 2026 report and negotiating mandate

    2027–2028 mandate to negotiate an instrument on autonomous weapons.

06 · Method and limits

How it is verified

The chain of proof

  • 42 records in catalog/instruments/, each with source, access date and verification level.
  • 16 full texts preserved; 15 originals with SHA-256 in catalog/acquisitions.json and in the manifest.
  • 10 texts read end-to-end; 32 records verified at metadata level; 0 sources located.
  • Citable units with character offsets and page numbers; the build is deterministic and offline.

What is missing

  • CETS 225 is not in force: 21 signatures, 2 ratifications.
  • WAICO is not in force: 38 reported founding members; no deposited ratification was verified.
  • Two AI-specific treaties: CETS 225 and the WAICO Agreement. This does not mean no others exist, but that no other has been located and verified.
  • No international complaint, sanction or judicial review mechanism is established by these instruments.
  • Latin America, the Middle East and Central Asia remain uncovered by verified regional instruments.
  • ISO/IEC standards are paywalled: metadata only. English texts only; no translation is presented as authentic.
  • No national implementation or compliance data.
